                                   Introduction

         The Thai Ministry of Education has reformed the English curriculum
to include communicative and 21st-century skills. Nevertheless, many schools
still prioritize memorization and examination over the practical use of the
language (Ministry of Education, Thailand, 2021). Previous research indicates
that Thai students struggle to use English in real-life communication, despite
their knowledge of grammatical rules (Mala & Jikkham, 2016). Thus, it is
necessary to reconsider the role of grammar instruction and how it should be
taught in the EFL context to equip students with the skills they need for real-
life communication. Ur (2011) and Willis (1996) suggested future directions
for grammar teaching within a task-based communicative approach.
         A review of the existing literature indicates that task-based grammar
instruction in the Thai context often exhibits limited integration of task-based and
grammar instruction, especially in enhancing multiple dimensions of students'
communicative competence, as outlined in Celce-Murcia's (2007) model of
communicative competence. To provide a task-based grammar lesson, the
TBLT framework by Willis (1996) has been used in previous studies on
grammar instruction in the EFL context for high school learners (e.g., Yildiz
& Senel, 2017) and for university learners (e.g., Thompson & Millington,
2012); however, these studies did not explore students’ communicative
competence. The TBLT framework by Willis (1996) has also been used to
enhance students’ communicative competence in the EFL context, such as
by Waluyo (2019). Nevertheless, these studies did not integrate grammar
instruction into the task-based framework, resulting in limited insight into
how this integration could influence the development of communicative
competence.

        Although previous studies (e.g., Thompson & Millington, 2012;
Waluyo, 2019; Willis, 1996; Yildiz & Senel, 2017) have shown the potential
advantages of TBLT, the integration of task-based grammar instruction to
improve both linguistic accuracy and the multiple dimensions of
communicative competence has not been thoroughly examined.
Furthermore, there is a lack of studies exploring students' perceptions of task-
based grammar instruction and teachers' reflections on its implementation,
especially within the Thai educational context.
        To address these gaps in the literature, three research questions were
formulated as follows:
        1. What effect does task-based grammar instruction have on students’
communicative competence?
        2. What are the students’ perceptions of task-based grammar
instruction in helping them enhance their communicative competence?
        3. What insights does the teacher gain from reflecting on the
implementation of task-based grammar instruction aimed at enhancing
students’ communicative competence?

                                Literature Review

Task-Based Grammar Instruction

         Fotos and Ellis (1991) suggested that grammar tasks promoted
discussion of grammar and helped EFL learners increase their knowledge of a
difficult L2 rule. Grammar tasks must be designed to raise the learner’s
consciousness about the grammatical properties of the L2 and to incorporate
a multi-way information gap. Grammar tasks can be practiced in teacher-
directed lessons or in pair/group work to increase opportunities for
negotiating meaning. According to Ur (2018), it is necessary to balance
explicit grammar teaching with opportunities for meaningful language use.
To illustrate, explicit instruction is paired with meaningful use, and grammar
activities should be embedded within tasks that require authentic
communication rather than isolated from communicative contexts. This
point of view aligns with the core basis of task-based language teaching
(TBLT) and other scholars (Ellis et al., 2022; Larsen-Freeman, 2020).
         Task-based grammar instruction can enhance the multidimensional
components of communicative competence outlined by Celce-Murcia (2007)
since TBLT provides students with exposure to grammatical forms and
vocabulary through meaningful communication (Ellis, 2003). Tasks often
elicit the use of strategies (Nakatani, 2010). Students practice fixed
expressions and formulaic language, as tasks often involve greetings, requests,
and routines (Boers & Lindstromberg, 2012). Engaging in pair and group

tasks can help students improve the skills needed to manage interactions
smoothly (Hall, 2011). Tasks are situated in culturally relevant scenarios that
require students to consider their language use and adapt it to social norms,
roles, and expectations, preparing them to communicate appropriately in
different sociocultural contexts (Celce-Murcia, 2007). Task-based instruction
fosters students' ability to organize and connect ideas as they attempt to
accomplish tasks such as discussion, storytelling, or problem-solving, thereby
improving discourse competence (Willis & Willis, 2007).
        The present study proposes a conceptual framework for task-based
grammar instruction by integrating Communicative Language Teaching with
communicative, grammar-based tasks (Fotos & Ellis, 1991) and the Task-
Based Language Teaching (TBLT) framework (Willis, 1996). This conceptual
framework aims to provide grammar instruction that enhances the
multidimensional communicative competence of lower-secondary EFL
students in a Fundamental English 3 course, as shown in Figure 1.

Communicative Competence

         Different models have been constructed to assess students’
communicative competence (e.g., Celce-Murcia, 2007; Celce-Murcia et al.,
1995). Communicative competence is recognized as a multidimensional
construct. Savignon (1997) emphasized that communicative competence is
shaped by political and ideological forces, particularly the concept of
“choice,” which influences classroom practices and the negotiation of
meaning and power. Although this study does not explicitly analyze the
political dimension of communicative competence, this decision was made to
maintain a focused scope on the linguistic and pedagogical aspects relevant
to the research objectives. Nevertheless, the study recognizes that
communicative competence is influenced by social and political factors and
is not a value-free concept, and that ideas about power, identity, and
individual choice are naturally part of how communicative competence is
understood and applied in the classroom.
         Based on a comparison of different models of communicative
competence, the revised model proposed by Marianne Celce-Murcia (2007)
was selected to assess students’ communicative competence because it
provides detailed descriptions of each component of communicative
competence and expands upon the earlier model by Marianne Celce-Murcia
et al. (1995). These revisions include the addition of formulaic competence,
three additional learning strategies within strategic competence, and
interactional competence.

Previous Studies on Task-Based Grammar Instruction in Enhancing
Communicative Competence

        Yildiz and Senel (2017) examined the impact of TBLT on students'
understanding of grammar during grammar instruction. This investigation
involved 32 eighth-grade students over a period of 2.5 months. The findings
suggested that TBLT significantly enhanced students' grammar knowledge in
the experimental group and produced meaningful outcomes compared to
traditional language-teaching methods.
        Somawati et al. (2018) conducted a study to explore the extent to
which TBLT is effective in enhancing learners' communicative competence.
A total of 62 students from the Tourism department, across two classes,
participated in the study. The treatment consisted of 10 lessons from an
English for Tourism module designed with a TBLT approach. The findings
indicated that TBLT was beneficial for enhancing learners' communicative
competence, particularly regarding fluency and one aspect of accuracy,
namely complexity.

         A study conducted by Waluyo (2019) used theme-based role-plays to
foster EFL learners' communicative competence within a task-based
framework. The study investigated the progress of 782 students in their
theme-based role-play activities over a 12-week academic term and assessed
the impact on their performance in the final speaking examination. The
results supported the hypothesis that students’ performance in theme-based
role-play improves their communicative competence.

                             Research Methodology

Research Design

         The study used a one-group pre-test/post-test experimental mixed-
methods design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018), employing both quantitative and
qualitative data collection methods. Quantitative data were collected through
pretests and posttests of an English-speaking test, while qualitative data were
gathered from the English-speaking test, semi-structured interviews, and the
teacher’s reflective journals, which were used to provide in-depth
explanations to support the quantitative findings.

Participants

        The study involved 30 eighth-grade students in a Fundamental
English 3 course during the first semester of the academic year 2025 at a
demonstration school in Bangkok, Thailand. The students were selected using
the convenience sampling technique. The researcher was assigned to teach 30
students during the semester. The students were heterogeneous in terms of
their academic achievement and level of English proficiency (A1-A2) based
on the CEFR in the Basic Education curriculum.

Data Collection and Research Instruments

        Data collection was conducted over 16 weeks during the first
semester of the academic year 2025. Three research instruments and one
instructional instrument were validated by three experts and then used in the
study as follows:

used to assess students' communicative competence in the pretest and
posttest. There were twenty-two items in total. The total score is twenty-two
points from the total subdimensions of each communicative competence as
follows: Linguistic Competence (3), Strategic Competence (5), Formulaic
Competence (4), Sociocultural Competence (3), Interactional Competence
(3), Discourse Competence (4). The researcher and the interrater rated each
item ‘FOUND (1)’ or ‘NOT FOUND (0)’ and took some notes to assess
students’ communicative competence. The constructed scale was validated by
the three experts and then piloted with characteristics similar to those of the
participants to assess its effectiveness.

Reflective Journals

        A teacher’s reflective journal was used to investigate what the teacher
learned from implementing task-based grammar instruction to improve
students’ communicative competence. The reflection questions were
reviewed by the experts to assess content validity and revised accordingly.
Thus, six reflective questions were formulated to provide vivid and useful
insights into how task-based grammar instruction works in practice, how it
improves communicative competence, the components of communicative
competence, the challenges it faces, potential solutions, and suggestions for
future lessons.

Semi-Structured Focus Group Interviews

        A semi-structured focus group interview was used to investigate
students’ perceptions of task-based grammar instruction in helping them
improve their communicative competence. The interview questions were
reviewed by the experts and revised based on their suggestions. To gain in-
depth, useful information from participants with varying communicative
competence, three focus group interviews were conducted. Each focus group
consisted of six participants sharing a characteristic regarding their
improvement in communicative competence, as determined by comparing
their pre-test and post-test results: large improvement, slight improvement,
or no improvement. Therefore, eighteen participants were purposively
selected for the interviews. Six interview questions were designed to
investigate students’ perceptions of task-based grammar instruction in
helping them improve their communicative competence.

Lesson Plans for Task-Based Grammar Instruction

        Twelve lesson plans for task-based grammar instruction were
developed based on the conceptual framework (Fotos & Ellis, 1991; Willis,
1996) and implemented for 12 weeks. Lesson plans were validated by the
experts and adjusted based on their comments and suggestions.

Data Analysis

         For quantitative analysis, descriptive statistics were used to reveal the
students’ communicative competence, and a paired-samples t-test was used
to determine whether there was a statistically significant difference between
the mean scores of students’ multidimensional communicative competence
before and after the implementation of task-based grammar instruction.
         In terms of qualitative analysis, descriptive analysis was used to
analyze the data from “the note part” on the constructed scale to describe the
communicative competence of students. Thematic analysis was used to reveal
students’ perceptions of task-based grammar instruction and the teacher's
reflections on its implementation.

                                        Findings

Effects of Task-Based Grammar Instruction on Students’
Multidimensional Communicative Competence

        The results of the students’ multidimensional communicative
competence were gained from the pre-test and the post-test scores on an
English-speaking test. The scores were calculated using a paired-samples t-
test. The results are presented in Table 2.

        As shown in Table 2, the mean scores of the pretest and the posttest
were 13.60 and 14.63, respectively. The average gain score was positive
(+1.03). The significance value was 0.01, which was lower than the

predetermined level of confidence at 0.05. Thus, there was a statistically
significant difference between the mean scores of multidimensional
communicative competence before and after the implementation of task-
based grammar instruction. The results revealed that task-based grammar
instruction improved the students’ multidimensional communicative
competence.
         Based on the pre-test and post-test results, the maximum scores
obtained were 18 for the pretest and 19 for the posttest. The minimum scores
were 7 for the pretest and 6 for the posttest. To determine improvements in
students’ multidimensional communicative competence, the criteria were
based on the difference between the pre-test and post-test scores, with the
highest score gain being +6 and the lowest score gain being −4. Six students
showed a large improvement, with their post-test scores increasing by 3
points or more. Among these six students, one increased by 6 points, two
increased by 4 points, and three increased by 3 points. Thirteen students
showed a slight improvement, with their post-test scores increasing by 1-2
points. Six of them increased by 2 points, and seven of them increased by 1
point. Eleven students showed no improvement, with their post-test scores
being equal to their pre-test scores and decreasing by 1 point or more. Among
these students, the post-test scores of six students were equal to their pre-test
scores. One student decreased by one point. Three students decreased by 2
points, and one student decreased by 4 points.
         Regarding the multiple dimensions of communicative competence,
‘interactional competence’ showed a statistically significant improvement.
There was improvement in its subdimensions, including ‘conversational
competence’ and ‘non-verbal/paralinguistic competence,’ with the average
gain score of +0.20, while ‘actional competence’ had no gain score. Thus,
students improved their conversational competence and non-
verbal/paralinguistic competence.
         There was an improvement in three subdimensions of ‘discourse
competence’, which are the use of ‘the deixis system,’ ‘temporal
continuity/shift,’ and the performance of ‘oral narrative of spoken genre,’
with the average gain scores at +0.17, +0.10, and +0.03, respectively, while
there was no improvement in the use of ‘a cohesive device.’ Therefore,
students used more of ‘the deixis system,’ ‘temporal continuity/shift,’ and
they performed the ‘oral narrative of the spoken genre’ better.
         Regarding ‘strategic competence,’ there was an improvement in its
two subdimensions, including the use of ‘stalling strategies’ and ‘self-
monitoring strategies,’ with average gain scores of +0.30 and +0.14,
respectively. In contrast, the three subdimensions, which include the use of
‘social strategies,’ ‘interacting strategies,’ and ‘achievement strategies,’
decreased, with average scores of -0.04, -0.07, and -0.17, respectively. Thus,

the students used more stalling and self-monitoring strategies in

use fewer social, interactional, and achievement strategies.
         There was an improvement in two subdimensions of ‘linguistic
competence,’ which are ‘the ability to use the morphological inflections’ and
‘the ability to construct grammatically correct and meaningful sentences using
basic sentence patterns and types,’ with average gain scores of +0.07 and
+0.03, respectively. While students improved these abilities, there was no
improvement in ‘the ability to use the lexical resources.’
         In terms of ‘formulaic competence,’ there was an improvement in one
subdimension, which is ‘the use of routines,’ with the average gain score of
+0.10. Thus, the students used more of ‘routines’ when communicating.
However, there was no improvement in the three subdimensions, which are
the use of ‘collocations,’ ‘idioms,’ and ‘lexical frames.’
         Regarding ‘sociocultural competence,’ there was no improvement in
its two subdimensions, including the awareness of ‘social contextual factors’
and ‘stylistic appropriateness factors.’ The average score for its subdimension,
the awareness of ‘cultural factors,’ decreased slightly by 0.03. The results
showed that the students tend to have less awareness of cultural factors.
         The quantitative findings will be further explained through qualitative
results to provide a more comprehensive illustration of the improvement in
students’ communicative competence.

Interactional Competence

        Six students improved their ‘conversational competence’ (S20, S6, S8,
S26, S2, S15). In the posttest, the students engaged more in the conversation,
asking their partners questions, collaborating, and backchanneling rather than
waiting for their partners to ask them questions, as found in the pretest. The
improvement is illustrated in the following excerpts from the post-test
conversation:

             Do you like this hobby?
             But I like it because I like to…. I like to study a new thing and
             I like music. I like running, yeah.
             (S6: large improvement)

        Improvement in ‘non-verbal/paralinguistic competence’ was evident
in six students (S26, S24, S19, S27, S14, S17). These students used or
demonstrated non-verbal turn-taking signals, backchannel behaviors,
gestures, eye contact, and haptic behavior, as shown in the excerpts from the
post-test conversation:

Discourse Competence

        Improvement in the use of ‘the deixis system’ was evident in the
posttest. Six students (S29, S6, S25, S26, S5, S30) used the deixis system in
discourse. The following excerpts serve as an example:
             I’m okay, but I’m feeling like I’m going to be sick because last
             night I didn’t sleep well. I’m thirteen years old this year.
             (S29: large improvement)

       Improvement in the use of ‘temporal continuity/shift’ was revealed
in the posttest. Four students (S24, S25, S23, S10) used ‘temporal
continuity/shift,’ as illustrated in the excerpt from post-test conversation
below:

             It depends on the person. If it is my friend, I prefer to
             spend time with them. But if I don’t really know them,
             I prefer to stay alone. (S10: no improvement)

        Three students (S24, S25, S30) improved their oral narrative
performance in the spoken genre. However, no improvement was seen
among students in the no-improvement group. Improvement was evident in
the excerpts from pre-test and post-test conversations:

             (pretest) playing sports and playing games.
             (posttest) I think playing sports and maybe playing
             games. And some would like to play music, sing a song.
             I like listening to music. (S25: large improvement)

Strategic Competence

         Improvement in the use of ‘stalling strategies’ was shown in the
posttest. Nine students (S20, S25, S29, S11, S26, S27, S1, S15, S21) used
stalling strategies, such as fillers, hesitation devices, gambits, and self-
repetition in the posttest.
         The students across all three improvement groups used ‘fillers and
hesitation devices,’ such as ‘um’ and ‘ah.’
         ‘Gambits,’ which were ‘I think’ and ‘I’m not sure,’ were used by one
student (S25) from the large improvement group and one student (S26) from
the slight improvement group. Gambits were not observed among students
in the no-improvement group.

             I’m not sure, but I think Ratchayotin.
             (S26: slight improvement)

        ‘Self-repetition’ was also used by one student (S29) from the large
improvement group and two students (S21, S26) from the slight
improvement group. Self-repetition was not observed among students in the
no-improvement group. The use of ‘self-repetition’ in the excerpt from the
post-test conversation is illustrated below:

             I love science because it’s…it’s interesting.
             (S21: slight improvement)

        Improvement in the use of ‘self-monitoring strategies’ was found in
the posttest. Nine students (S20, S6, S24, S29, S16, S3, S23, S11, S19) used
self-monitoring strategies in communication. Nevertheless, no improvement
was evident among the students in the no-improvement group.
        Five out of six students (S20, S6, S24, S29, S16) in the large
improvement group improved the use of ‘self-monitoring strategies,’ while
the other student (S25) did not illustrate the use of self-monitoring strategies
in the posttest. The use of ‘self-monitoring strategies’ is shown below:

             I like to be… I like to go shopping with my mom.
             How about watching a book…reading a book?
             (S29: large improvement)

       Four students (S3, S23, S11, S19) in the slight improvement group
improved the use of ‘self-monitoring strategies.’ Three of them (S3, S23, S11)
used self-initiated repair and self-rephrasing, while the other student (S19)
used other-initiated repair and self-rephrasing, as illustrated in the excerpts
below:
             Yeah, I like to… I really want to try to play the guitar, but
             it’s a bit hard and needs a lot of practice.
             (S23: slight improvement)

             Do you like to play soccer? (S19: slight improvement)
             Uh? (S20)
             Do you like to play football? (S19: slight improvement)
             Yes. (S20)

        From the conversation, the student (S20) expressed confusion and a
lack of understanding and asked for clarification. This caused the student
(S19) to reformulate his utterance to make the other student (S20) understand
by changing the word ‘soccer’ to ‘football,’ which was likely to be a more
familiar word for the student (S20).

        Although the use of ‘self-monitoring strategies’ did not improve
among students in the no-improvement group, one student (S15) monitored
their partner during the conversation, as illustrated below:
             Do you like playing games? Why or why not?
             (S5: no improvement)
             Do you like playing football? (S16)
             [in Thai] Answer the question first, I asked whether you like it
             or not. (S15: no improvement)
             I like playing games. (S16)

Linguistic Competence

         Improvement in students’ ability to use morphological inflections was
evident in the posttest, as two students (S2 and S12) from the slight
improvement group demonstrated more accurate verb inflections. These verb
inflections appeared not only in the past tense but also in the simple present
tense, as illustrated below:

             I was so bored.
             What she likes and how much money to pay.
             No, I don’t like to play sports.
             (S2: slight improvement)

        Improvement in students’ ability to construct grammatically correct
and meaningful sentences using basic sentence patterns and types was evident
in the posttest. Two students (S12 and S14) in the slight improvement group
produced more grammatically accurate and meaningful sentences in the
posttest, whereas they had produced only one sentence in the pretest:

             (pre-test) Ummm, seven am.
                        Study and talk with a friend.
                        Play a game, draw.

             (post-test) Because I love to spend time with my friends.
                         I love both, too. Because I prefer to be
                         alone. Because I love privacy.
                         (S12: slight improvement)

Formulaic Competence

        Improvement in ‘the use of routines’ was shown by two students
(S20, S28). The student (S20) in the large improvement group showed various
uses of routines to give a ‘formulaic response’ and ‘personal information’ and
to express ‘preferences’ and ‘reasons,’ as shown below:

       On the other hand, the student (S28) in the slight improvement group
only showed the use of routines to express ‘likes and dislikes,’ as shown

             I love music. I like sports. I like art. I don’t like reading.
             I don’t like playing games. (S28: slight improvement)

        Thus, the student (S20) from the large improvement group showed
more varied use of routines than the student (S28) in the slight improvement

        To further explore ‘formulaic competence,’ the results revealed that
every student demonstrated ‘the use of collocations’ in the posttest. Common
collocations used across all three groups of improvement were ‘playing
games,’ ‘listening to music,’ and ‘spending time with friends.’

Sociocultural Competence

        The decrease in ‘the awareness of cultural factors’ resulted from the
empirical findings that the student (S17) in the no-improvement group did
not demonstrate cultural factors and sociocultural norms typical of English-
speaking classrooms, such as making eye contact, participating actively, and
displaying open body language.

Students’ Perceptions of Task-Based Grammar Instruction

        To investigate the students’ perceptions of task-based grammar
instruction, three semi-structured focus group interviews were conducted,
and the transcriptions were analyzed using thematic analysis. Five themes
emerged across the different improvement groups.

Benefits of Task-Based Grammar Instruction

         Students across all improvement groups, particularly those with large
and slight improvement, often emphasized the value of using grammar in
real-life communicative contexts, noting opportunities to practice speaking
and observe how grammar is used in authentic conversations. An excerpt
from the conversation is shown below:

             When the teacher provides examples of grammar usage,
             students can see how these target grammatical forms are used
             in actual sentences and real conversations. I believe that if
             students are only taught the meaning of a word and are left to
             learn its usage on their own, they will not be able to use it
             fluently or as naturally as native speakers do in everyday
             situations, since native speakers do not always speak exactly as
             presented in textbooks. In my opinion, this teaching approach
             is more practical and effective, as it helps students internalize
             language concepts and apply them in spontaneous speech.
             (S25: large improvement)

        Students from all groups reported that task-based grammar
instruction expanded their vocabulary and grammatical awareness, which they
perceived as fundamental to communication.
        Many students, particularly in the slight improvement group,
highlighted that interactive lessons made learning more enjoyable and less
monotonous.

Challenges in Task-Based Grammar Instruction

        Across all groups, students reported difficulties understanding
different accents in the video clips used to introduce target grammatical
features in communicative contexts during the pre-task phase, and they also
had difficulties pronouncing new vocabulary learned in the lessons.
        Some students expressed concern about their peers’ lack of
confidence in speaking English.
        Some students struggled to form sentences, connect ideas when
narrating stories or experiences, and retrieve the right vocabulary in real time.
        Another challenge is the need to mentally translate from Thai to
English before speaking. This process slowed students’ responses and often
led to pauses.

Effects on Communicative Competence

     Most students reported an increased ability to use correct grammar in
communication.

             I am able to use correct grammar in my communication, and I
             can convey messages clearly without causing
             misunderstandings. (S29: large improvement)


         Some students acknowledged the usefulness of communication
strategies, such as using fillers and non-linguistic means.

The Role of Feedback

         Some students recognized the important role of teacher feedback in
their communicative competence, as it provided corrections and clarifications
of their understanding of target grammatical features and the effectiveness of
their communication.

Suggestions for Improvement

        The students made five suggestions across all groups, as follows:
‘incorporating games and interactive activities (e.g., Kahoot, Blooket, Bingo),’
‘using more engaging media (e.g., songs, movies),’ ‘providing more
vocabulary support and translations,’ ‘rotating partners/groups to increase
diversity and challenge,’ and ‘enhancing visual materials (more attractive
themed-based teaching slides).

Teacher’s Reflections

       To investigate what the teacher learned from implementing task-
based grammar instruction, 12 reflective journals were analyzed using
thematic analysis. Seven themes emerged across the twelve lesson reflections.

Importance of Lesson Plan Preparation and Task Design

        A detailed lesson plan and well-prepared teaching materials lead to
the successful implementation of task-based grammar instruction. A carefully
designed task is required to elicit all the multiple dimensions of
communicative competence.

Development of Students’ Communicative Competence

        Students consistently demonstrated all multiple dimensions of
communicative competence in the twelve lessons. An extract from one of the
twelve journals is as follows:
             Linguistic Competence: Students used ‘adjectives’ when
             describing places such as “I like quiet places because it makes
             me feel comfortable, like mountains,” and “I’m looking for a
             quiet and luxurious vacation.”
             Strategic Competence: Communication strategies were used,
             such as self-initiated repair and gambits: “It’s comfy…
             comfortable”. And “Nah… isn’t it too crowded?”
             Formulaic Competence: Students used ‘formulaic chunks’ such
             as “I’m not really into New Zealand.” “How about Japan?” “I
             don’t mind.” “That’s a great idea.” and “I think so.”
             Sociocultural Competence: Students expressed their messages
             appropriately within the overall social and cultural context.
             Students politely refused their friends: “Singapore is similar to
             Thailand and quite hot. How about Japan?” “No, it’s so
             expensive. Let’s go somewhere else.”, and “But I want to go
             somewhere adventurous. How about going to the mountain?”
             Interactional competence: Students engaged in interaction
             effectively according to the social and contextual aspects of
             communication. The use of gestures, eye contact, turn-taking,
             and topic shifting was demonstrated during the task.
             Discourse competence: Students used conjunctions in
             discourse: “I want to see the northern lights, which are
             considered exotic in Thailand, and the atmosphere is very
             relaxing.” “I like India because people are friendly and I love
             Indian civilization.” “I like quiet places because it makes me
             feel comfortable, like mountains. (Reflective Journal 6)

Student Engagement and Interaction

        The reflections showed that pair and small-group tasks tended to
enhance students’ participation and balance interaction compared to large-
group tasks, since some students dominated in the latter. Engaging tasks
promoted confidence, motivation, and a willingness to speak. However, some
students remained reluctant to interact in English, often providing short or
simple responses.

Challenges in the Integration of Grammar and Communicative
Competence

         Certain grammatical features, such as modals of prohibition and
obligation and the past perfect tense, were challenging for students to use in
the communicative, grammar-based tasks. There were also challenges with
similarities among certain grammatical features, such as the past simple, past
continuous, and past perfect tenses. Students expressed confusion about their
differences and how to use them, which affected their language accuracy and
appropriateness.

The Role of Authentic Materials and Contextualization

        Authentic materials, such as videos, audio, and real-life situations,
help students observe grammar in context and increase their engagement.
Students respond positively to real-world themes and scenarios, which
promotes meaningful communication and language transfer.

Challenges of Task-Based Grammar Instruction
        Time management within each task was a recurring issue: some pairs
finished quickly, while others took longer.
        Continuous professional development and updating instructional
approaches are needed for teachers to provide effective task-based grammar
instruction.
        Some students still did not elaborate or ask follow-up questions,
which hindered the depth of interaction.

Suggestions for Future Practice
        The reflections provide suggestions for future practice. Firstly,
communication strategies should be explicitly taught alongside grammatical
features to equip students with what they need for communication. Secondly,
tasks should be varied, relevant, and appropriately challenging, providing

modeling and exposure to target grammatical features support students’
learning. Lastly, pair tasks are often more effective for balanced interaction
and elicit more of each student’s communicative competence.

                         Discussions and Implications

Research Question 1: What effect does task-based grammar
instruction have on students’ communicative competence?

         Analysis of students’ pre-test and post-test scores indicated a
statistically significant improvement in multidimensional communicative
competence from the implementation of task-based grammar instruction.
The most significant gains were observed in ‘interactional competence,’
indicating that engaging students in authentic, task-based activities
particularly enhanced their ability to manage real-life communication
scenarios. Improvements were also found in ‘discourse competence,’
‘strategic competence,’ ‘linguistic competence,’ and ‘formulaic competence,’
although these did not reach statistical significance. This may be due to the
specific design of the tasks or the relatively short implementation duration,
which may not have provided sufficient opportunities for students to develop
these components of communicative competence. Future studies could
explore how modifications to task design or a longer intervention duration
might yield greater improvements across these components. In contrast, a
decrease in ‘sociocultural competence’ was observed. This finding may
indicate that the tasks used did not sufficiently address sociocultural and
pragmatic elements of communication. In addition, the variation in
improvement across components may be attributed to individual differences
among learners or to the complexity of developing these aspects within the
study’s time frame. In view of this, future instructional designs should
incorporate cultural and pragmatic elements into task-based grammar
instruction to address cultural norms, values, and context-specific language
use, and should also tailor pedagogical strategies to accommodate learners’
diverse needs and enhance less responsive components of communicative
competence.
         Qualitative data from student interviews and the teacher’s reflective
journals support these quantitative results, with many students reporting
greater confidence and an increased ability to interact using English.
Nevertheless, a few students had difficulty adapting to culturally specific
communicative situations, reflecting the quantitative decrease in sociocultural
competence. These findings are consistent with previous studies (Somawati
et al., 2018; Huang, 2016), which also found that TBLT is effective in

enhancing communicative competence. Particularly in the Asian context, this
study aligns with Nghia and Quang’s (2021) critical review of studies,
indicating that task-based grammar instruction can significantly improve
communicative competence. Nevertheless, it is vital for future research to
investigate how task-based approaches can be developed to improve all
dimensions of communicative competence, particularly sociocultural
competence.

Research Question 2: What are the students’ perceptions of task-based
grammar instruction in helping them enhance their communicative
competence?

        Data from the three semi-structured focus group interviews were
analyzed to answer this question. The findings revealed that students had
positive perceptions of task-based grammar instruction. The results of the
study align with those of Thompson and Millington (2012) and Marlina
(2014), revealing the effectiveness of task-based instruction in improving
students’ grammar mastery and in the application of grammar in speaking.
The results are also consistent with Yildiz and Senel (2017), who found that
task-based instruction improved students’ motivation by enhancing their
interest in the language, enjoyment of learning, student engagement, and
learning autonomy. The study's findings revealed the challenges students
encounter, particularly in listening, pronunciation, and language production.
The results of the study are consistent with those of Mala and Jikkham (2016),
which suggest that persistent, unsatisfactory situations exist, as some students
had difficulty communicating in real-life English situations.
        Students' suggestions for future task-based grammar instruction
indicate a need to emphasize greater engagement, support, and variety in
instructional design. The results of the study are consistent with those of
Waluyo (2019), highlighting teacher support as an important factor in the
effectiveness of task-based language teaching in fostering communicative
competence. Furthermore, it is essential to encourage a variety of
communication styles to promote students’ learning (Willis, 1996). Future
research could address these challenges by implementing task-based grammar
instruction that promotes greater student engagement, increased teacher
support, and a wider range of instructional designs.

Research Question 3: What insights does the teacher gain from
reflecting on the implementation of task-based grammar instruction
aimed at enhancing students’ communicative competence?”

         The findings indicate the importance of detailed lesson planning and
careful task design for the successful implementation of task-based grammar
instruction. The results are consistent with Willis and Willis (2007), who argue
that tasks play an important role in task-based lessons and that it is essential
to design task-like activities that involve authentic language use.
         The results revealed that task-based grammar instruction elicited each
of the multiple dimensions of communicative competence, consistent with
Celce-Murcia's (2007) model of communicative competence. Thus, the
results indicate the holistic development of communicative competence,
which aligns with Thomas and Reinders (2010), who assert that TBLT adopts
a broad view of language development in which different skills are integrated
and required for the completion of various learning activities.
         The reflections show that pair and small-group tasks can enhance
student participation, confidence, and willingness to speak, whereas larger-
group tasks can limit some students' engagement. The findings are consistent
with those of Yildiz and Senel (2017), who found that students gained
confidence in using the target language to accomplish the task. The analysis
of the reflections also indicates ongoing challenges in integrating complex or
closely related grammatical features into communicative tasks. Thus, explicit
contrastive instruction and scaffolded practice are required to help students
use the target grammatical features accurately and appropriately. This is
supported by Skehan (1996a), who contends that ‘a focus on form’ can
facilitate language learning. Based on the reflections, the use of authentic
materials played an important role in student engagement and contextualized
language learning. The findings are consistent with Celce-Murcia (2007),
suggesting that well-contextualized and meaningful materials and authentic
tasks are essential for task-based grammar instruction.
         The analysis highlights the value of ongoing reflective practice and
professional development. The findings align with Bolton (2010), implying
that a reflective journal helps teachers become aware of their current practice
by providing opportunities to reflect, analyze, and improve their teaching
practice. Future research could further examine the transferability of these
lessons across contexts and investigate how ongoing teacher reflection
influences long-term instructional effectiveness and students’
multidimensional communicative competence.

                     Limitations and Recommendations
                            for Future Research

         Although this study achieved its purposes, there were some
limitations during the research process. Subsequently, recommendations for
further research are proposed as follows:
         This study employed a one-group pretest and posttest experimental
mixed-methods design; a comparison between a control group and an
experimental group could not be made. Thus, a pretest-posttest control group
design is recommended for future research, using random sampling and
random assignment.
         The present study used a relatively small sample size of 30 students,
selected through convenience sampling. As a result, the sample may not be
representative of the larger student population, and the findings may not be
generalizable to other groups. Thus, a larger sample size and random
sampling are recommended.
         This research was conducted for sixteen weeks with twelve task-based
grammar lessons; a longer period and an extended process may be required
for students to improve all six components of communicative competence.
Future research could extend the data-collection period and conduct more
task-based grammar lessons to examine whether students can improve all six
components of communicative competence.

                                       Conclusion

         This study found that task-based grammar instruction significantly
enhanced students’ multidimensional communicative competence, and that
students had positive perceptions of it, recognizing its benefits. The teacher’s
reflections highlighted the importance of detailed lesson planning and careful
task design for successful task-based grammar instruction. The improvement
in multiple dimensions of students’ communicative competence as evidenced
in the reflective journals emphasizes the value of an ongoing reflective
practice for improving task-based grammar instruction and promoting
professional development.
